title: Cloud Security
summary: Secure cloud identity, networks, data and workloads, and investigate cloud incidents. Cloud-neutral principles first. Curriculum in development.
description: A programme that teaches cloud-neutral security principles first, then clearly labelled provider-specific examples from AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. Essential activities use supplied data and simulators, so you never need to create paid cloud resources. Each module has an authored starter lesson; full lessons, the remaining labs and the examination are in development.
outcomes: Use cloud audit logs for detection
inclusions: IAM review and audit-log labs available now
Final examination, badge and certificate when complete

faqs.q: Do I need a paid cloud account?
faqs.a: No. Essential activities use supplied datasets and simulators. Any optional exercises in a real cloud account will be clearly labelled, with cost warnings.

badge.name: AMANIQ Cloud Security
badge.description: Awarded for completing the AMANIQ Academy Cloud Security programme.
badge.criteria: Complete all required lessons and labs and score at least 75% on the final examination.

modules.title: Cloud Computing and the Shared Responsibility Model
modules.purpose:
Kanem's board is moving three systems to the cloud and one director believes "the provider looks after security". This module gives you the precise vocabulary (characteristics, service and deployment models), the structures that shape cloud security (regions, accounts and hierarchies), the shared responsibility model service by service, the basics of cloud governance, and answers to the most common misconceptions. You finish by mapping responsibilities for four real-looking workloads and briefing the CFO.

**To complete this module:** finish all five lessons and pass the lab (80%), including the written briefing.
modules.prerequisiteKnowledge: General IT knowledge. No prior cloud experience is required.
objectives: Classify cloud services by characteristics, service model and deployment model
Design an account, subscription or project structure that limits blast radius and respects data-location requirements
Assign security responsibilities to provider, customer or both for IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
Recommend first governance decisions and preventive guardrails
Correct common cloud security misconceptions with precise reasoning
assessmentCriteria: Correctly maps responsibilities across service models
Attributes incidents to the failing side of the model
Explains residual responsibilities clearly to an executive
modules.instructorNotes: Estimated time: 2.5 hours of lessons plus 1 hour of lab.

lessons.title: What cloud computing is: characteristics, service and deployment models
objectives: Identify the five essential characteristics of cloud computing and their security consequences
Classify a service as IaaS, PaaS or SaaS
Distinguish public, private, community and hybrid deployments

checks.question: Kanem moves staff email to Microsoft 365. Which service model is this?
checks.explanation: A complete application delivered by the provider is SaaS.

checks.question: Which characteristic explains why anyone with permissions can create an exposed resource in seconds?
checks.explanation: Self-service is what makes the cloud fast, and why identity and guardrails matter.

checks.question: A sudden spike in compute costs at 03:00 could indicate which security problems? Select all that apply.
options: Resources launched by an unauthorised user
checks.explanation: Measured service makes unusual consumption visible; cost anomalies are a useful security signal.

lessons.title: Regions, accounts and the resource hierarchy
objectives: Explain regions and zones and when each improves resilience
Recognise data location as a legal and compliance decision
Design an account, subscription or project structure that limits blast radius

checks.question: Why should production and development run in separate accounts, subscriptions or projects?
options: It limits the blast radius: access and mistakes in one do not reach the other, and production can have stricter guardrails
checks.explanation: Accounts, subscriptions and projects are strong isolation boundaries.

checks.question: A policy assigned at the top of the hierarchy (organisation or management group) applies to:
checks.explanation: Policies and permissions are inherited downwards in all three providers.

checks.question: Who should be involved in choosing the region for customer personal data?
options: Only the engineer creating the resource
Nobody: the default region is fine
checks.explanation: Data-protection law and sector regulation affect where personal data may be stored and transferred.

lessons.title: The shared responsibility model, service by service
objectives: Assign responsibilities to provider, customer or both for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
Identify the responsibilities that always remain with the customer
Explain genuinely shared responsibilities such as backups, patching and encryption

checks.question: Kanem's reporting server runs on a cloud VM (IaaS). An attacker exploits a six-month-old operating-system vulnerability. Whose responsibility was the patch?
checks.explanation: In IaaS the customer manages the guest operating system.

checks.question: Which responsibilities stay with the customer in every model, including SaaS? Select all that apply.
options: Who has access and with which permissions
Classifying and protecting the data stored
Configuring the settings the service exposes, such as MFA and sharing
checks.explanation: Identities, data and configuration are always the customer's. Hypervisors are always the provider's.

checks.question: A managed database service takes automatic backups. What is still Kanem's job?
options: Setting retention, protecting backups from deletion and testing restores
checks.explanation: Backups are shared: the provider takes them, the customer configures, protects and tests them.

lessons.title: Cloud governance and adoption risks
objectives: Identify the main risks of rapid cloud adoption
Separate governance decisions from automated guardrails
Select first preventive guardrails for a new cloud environment

checks.question: Which control stops even an account administrator from disabling audit logging?
options: An organisation-level guardrail such as an AWS SCP, Azure Policy deny or Google organisation policy
A tag on the log bucket
checks.explanation: Guardrails applied above the account cannot be overridden from inside it.

checks.question: Which are sensible first guardrails before the first production workload? Select all that apply.
options: Block public storage unless an exception is approved
Allow every service so teams are not slowed down
checks.explanation: A few high-value preventive guardrails stop the most common and most damaging mistakes.

checks.question: Which NIST CSF 2.0 function covers organisational context, risk strategy, roles and policy?
checks.explanation: CSF 2.0 added Govern, which frames how cloud adoption is decided and overseen.

lessons.title: Seven cloud security misconceptions
objectives: Explain why common cloud security beliefs are incomplete
Respond to a misconception with a precise question or statement
Relate each misconception to the shared responsibility model

checks.question: "Our provider has ISO/IEC 27001, so our deployment is compliant." What is wrong?
options: The certificate covers the provider's controls in scope, not how the customer configured its own account
ISO/IEC 27001 does not apply to cloud providers
checks.explanation: Provider attestations are evidence about the provider. The customer must evidence its own side.

checks.question: Why doesn't encryption at rest protect a bucket that has been made public?
options: The service decrypts data for any request it authorises; encryption at rest protects the physical media
Encryption only works in private subnets
checks.explanation: Access control decides who receives decrypted data through the API.

checks.question: A database is in a private subnet. How could it still be reached? Select all that apply.
options: Through the provider's management API with valid credentials
Through a compromised application that can reach it
Through the internet, because private subnets are public
Through an overly broad network rule from another network
checks.explanation: Network placement is one layer; identities, applications and other rules provide other paths.

modules.title: Cloud Identity and Access Management
modules.purpose:
Kanem Financial Services' invoice application is about to go live in the cloud with a policy "copied from a tutorial". In this module you learn how cloud identities authenticate, how AWS, Azure and Google Cloud decide what an identity may do, how to apply least privilege with evidence, how workloads should get credentials, and how attackers escalate privileges. You finish with a real-looking access review.

**To complete this module:** finish all five lessons and pass the lab (80%), including the policy you write and your written finding.
modules.prerequisiteKnowledge: Cloud service models and shared responsibility (module 1). Comfortable reading JSON.
objectives: Distinguish authentication from authorisation and classify cloud principals
Predict access decisions from AWS IAM policies and explain Azure RBAC and Google Cloud IAM inheritance
Design least-privilege permissions from documented needs and usage evidence
Recommend workload identity mechanisms instead of long-lived keys
Identify privilege-escalation and defence-evasion permissions and design privileged access controls
keyConcepts: Explicit deny, allow and implicit deny
assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies excessive, escalation and evasion permissions
Writes a policy that passes all hidden access tests
Interprets access-activity evidence and escalates appropriately
Communicates the finding clearly to a manager
modules.instructorNotes: Estimated time: 2.75 hours of lessons plus 1.5 hours of lab. The 28 February PassRole activity seeds the module 9 incident.

lessons.title: Identities, authentication and authorisation in the cloud
objectives: Classify human, group and workload principals across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
Distinguish authentication from authorisation in a cloud API request
Recommend controls for human access (federation, MFA, groups, protected root accounts)

checks.question: A user signs in with a password and MFA, then deletes a production database they should never have been able to touch. Which control failed?
checks.explanation: The user proved who they were; the problem is that policy allowed the action. MFA does not reduce what an authenticated identity is allowed to do.

checks.question: Which practices improve human access to a cloud environment? Select all that apply.
options: Single sign-on from the corporate identity provider
Granting permissions to groups rather than individuals
Sharing one administrator account among the IT team
Using the root or Global Administrator account only for tasks that require it
checks.explanation: Federation, groups and a protected top-level account are standard guidance. Shared accounts destroy accountability and are hard to protect.

checks.question: In AWS, an IAM role is best described as:
options: A set of permissions that a person or service assumes temporarily
checks.explanation: Roles have no long-term password; principals assume them and receive temporary credentials.

lessons.title: How cloud access policies are evaluated
objectives: Read an IAM policy statement as Effect, Action, Resource and Condition
Predict AWS decisions using explicit deny, allow and implicit deny
Explain how scope and inheritance work in Azure RBAC and Google Cloud IAM

checks.question: A policy allows "s3:*" on "arn:aws:s3:::kanem-invoices/*" and denies "s3:DeleteObject" on the same resource. What happens to a DeleteObject request on an invoice?
options: Denied, because an explicit deny overrides any allow
Allowed if the user has MFA
Denied only if no other policy allows it
checks.explanation: In AWS evaluation an explicit deny always wins, regardless of allows elsewhere.

checks.question: Policy: Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::kanem-invoices/*. Which requests are denied? Select all that apply.
checks.code:
Request A: s3:GetObject  arn:aws:s3:::kanem-invoices/2026/inv-1.pdf
Request B: s3:GetObject  arn:aws:s3:::kanem-payroll/march.csv
Request C: s3:ListBucket arn:aws:s3:::kanem-invoices
Request D: s3:PutObject  arn:aws:s3:::kanem-invoices/2026/inv-2.pdf
checks.explanation: Only A matches both the action and the resource. B is another bucket, C is a different action on the bucket ARN, D is a different action. All three are implicitly denied.

checks.question: In Azure, a user is assigned Contributor on a subscription. What access do they have to a resource group inside it?
options: None, unless also assigned on the resource group
Contributor, because assignments are inherited by child scopes
Owner, because subscription roles are promoted
checks.explanation: Azure RBAC assignments apply at their scope and every scope beneath it.

lessons.title: Least privilege in practice
objectives: Derive the minimum permissions for a workload from its documented needs
Recognise dangerous wildcards and broad built-in roles
Use usage evidence and access reviews to remove unneeded permissions

checks.question: Which statement is the least privileged way to let an application store generated invoices?
checks.explanation: One action, scoped to the one prefix the application writes to.

checks.question: Which of these are reasonable ways to find and remove unused permissions? Select all that apply.
options: IAM last-accessed information or Access Analyzer unused-access findings in AWS
Asking each developer which permissions they would like
Regular access reviews where the owner confirms each grant
checks.explanation: Usage evidence and owner-confirmed reviews remove excess. Wish lists add it.

checks.question: Why must tags be protected when access decisions use them (ABAC)?
options: If a user can change a resource's tags, they may be able to change who can access it
Tags are not supported in Azure
checks.explanation: In ABAC, attributes are part of the policy. Whoever controls the attributes controls access.

lessons.title: Workload identities and temporary credentials
objectives: Explain the risks of long-lived access keys and client secrets
Choose the right workload identity mechanism in each provider
Respond to an exposed access key

checks.question: An application on an Azure VM needs to read from a storage account. What is the best way for it to authenticate?
options: Store the storage account key in the application settings
Use a managed identity for the VM with a role scoped to that storage account
checks.explanation: A managed identity removes stored secrets; the scoped role keeps it least privilege.

checks.question: You discover a valid cloud access key committed to a Git repository eight months ago. What should you do first?
options: Delete the file from the latest commit
Deactivate the key, then investigate its use in the audit logs
checks.explanation: Clones and forks already hold copies, so the key must be treated as compromised and disabled before anything else.

checks.question: What is the critical security control in workload identity federation for a CI pipeline?
options: The length of the access key
The trust rule that says which issuer, repository and branch may obtain credentials
checks.explanation: Federation is only as strong as the conditions on the trust rule. "Any repository" is effectively public access.

lessons.title: Privileged access and privilege escalation
objectives: Identify permissions that enable privilege escalation in each provider
Explain the iam:PassRole escalation path
Design privileged access with just-in-time elevation, break-glass accounts and guardrails

checks.question: Which permissions should be treated as administrative because they allow privilege escalation? Select all that apply.
options: iam:CreatePolicyVersion on a policy attached to yourself
checks.explanation: Editing your own policy, writing role assignments and passing any role all let an identity gain more access. Reading objects in one bucket does not.

checks.question: An identity has ec2:RunInstances and iam:PassRole on *. Why is this dangerous?
options: It can launch an instance with an administrator role attached and use that role's credentials
It can read every bucket directly
checks.explanation: The identity can create compute that holds more privilege than it has, then use it.

checks.question: What makes a break-glass account safe enough to keep?
options: Strong credentials stored offline, exclusion from controls that could lock everyone out, and an alert on every use
It is shared with all administrators
It is only used by contractors
checks.explanation: Break-glass accounts exist for emergencies, so they must be protected and every use must be noticed.

modules.title: Secure Cloud Networking
modules.purpose: Segment cloud networks and control exposure.
objectives: Design virtual networks and subnets.
Configure security groups and network ACLs.
Use private endpoints and secure admin access.
assessmentCriteria: Demonstrates the ability to design virtual networks and subnets.
Demonstrates the ability to configure security groups and network ACLs.
Demonstrates the ability to use private endpoints and secure admin access.

lessons.title: Virtual network design
objectives: Design virtual networks and subnets.

modules.title: Cloud Data Protection and Cryptography
modules.purpose:
Nobody at Kanem is sure what the loan-documents bucket holds or how it is protected, until a check finds it publicly readable. This module covers classifying and discovering data, encryption and key management, secrets management, preventing public storage access, and backups that survive an attacker. You finish by remediating the exposed bucket.

**To complete this module:** finish all five lessons and pass the lab (80%), including the written remediation plan.
modules.prerequisiteKnowledge: Modules 1 and 2 (shared responsibility, identity and access).
objectives: Classify cloud data and confirm its location with discovery tools
Choose encryption and key management options appropriate to data sensitivity
Design secrets management with identity-based access and rotation
Prevent public storage access and choose safer sharing patterns
Design backups and recovery with tested restores
Respond to and remediate a data exposure
keyConcepts: Encryption in transit and at rest
assessmentCriteria: Classifies data correctly
Identifies the configuration causes of an exposure
Orders containment, evidence and notification steps correctly
Writes a complete remediation plan
modules.instructorNotes: Estimated time: 2.5 hours of lessons plus 1.25 hours of lab.

lessons.title: Data classification, discovery and retention
objectives: Apply a classification scheme to cloud data stores
Use discovery tools to confirm where sensitive data lives
Set retention and minimisation rules with legal input

checks.question: Public website images and scanned customer ID cards are in the same bucket. What is the main problem?
options: One set of access rules must fit both, so either the website breaks or the ID scans are over-exposed
checks.explanation: Keep different classifications in separate stores so each gets the right controls.

checks.question: A discovery tool flags national ID numbers in a "test" bucket. What should you do?
options: Ignore it: discovery tools are always wrong
Treat it as a lead: review it, and if real, classify, restrict or delete the data
Make the bucket public to check
checks.explanation: Findings need human review; real sensitive data in test stores is a common exposure.

checks.question: Why does data minimisation reduce risk?
options: Data you no longer hold cannot be exposed or stolen
checks.explanation: Retention rules and deleting copies shrink the impact of any future incident.

lessons.title: Encryption and key management
objectives: Distinguish what encryption in transit and at rest protect against
Choose between provider-managed, customer-managed and external keys
Explain envelope encryption
Apply key management practices: separation of duties, rotation, logging, deletion protection

checks.question: What does a customer-managed key add to a restricted storage bucket?
options: A second, independent permission check (use of the key) and a precise audit trail of decryption
checks.explanation: Reading requires storage permission and key permission, and key use is logged.

checks.question: Which are sound key management practices? Select all that apply.
options: Separate who administers a key from who uses it
checks.explanation: Deleting a key destroys access to its data, so deletion must be tightly controlled.

checks.question: In envelope encryption, what does the key service's master key encrypt?
options: Every byte of the data directly
The data keys that encrypt the data
checks.explanation: Data keys encrypt data; the master (key-encryption) key protects the data keys and never leaves the service.

lessons.title: Secrets management
objectives: Identify unsafe places for secrets
Design secret storage with identity-based access, logging and rotation
Plan detection and response for leaked secrets

checks.question: Where should an application's partner API key be stored?
options: In a secrets manager, read at run time with the application's workload identity
checks.explanation: A secrets manager gives access control, encryption, logging and rotation.

checks.question: Which events should trigger an immediate secret rotation? Select all that apply.
options: A person who knew the secret leaves
Suspected exposure in a code repository
A scheduled rotation date is reached
checks.explanation: Restarts are not a reason; departures, suspected exposure and schedules are.

checks.question: What catches secrets before they reach a shared repository?
options: Secret scanning in commits and the CI pipeline
checks.explanation: Scanning blocks or flags credentials at commit and build time.

lessons.title: Preventing public storage access
objectives: Explain the layers that decide access to cloud storage
Enable and enforce public-access prevention in each provider
Choose safer sharing patterns than public buckets
Outline the first response to a storage exposure

checks.question: Which control stops a bucket policy from granting public access even if someone writes one?
options: Account- or organisation-level public access prevention (for example S3 Block Public Access)
checks.explanation: Public-access guardrails override resource policies that would grant public access.

checks.question: A partner needs one report file for a day. What is the safest approach?
options: Make the bucket public for a day
A time-limited signed link to that one object
Copy the file to a personal account
checks.explanation: Signed links are scoped, expiring and logged.

checks.question: A restricted bucket is found publicly readable. What comes first?
options: Block public access, then preserve logs and work out what was accessed
Rotate every password in the company
checks.explanation: Stop the exposure, keep the evidence, then scope the impact with the DPO and legal.

lessons.title: Backup, retention and recovery
objectives: Design backups that survive compromised administrator credentials
Set RPO and RTO with the business
Plan and record restore tests

checks.question: Why store backups in a separate account with different administrators?
options: An attacker or mistake in the production account cannot also delete the backups
checks.explanation: Separation limits the blast radius of a compromise to production only.

checks.question: The business accepts losing at most one hour of invoice data. What does that define?
checks.explanation: RPO is the acceptable data loss measured in time; RTO is the acceptable downtime.

checks.question: What proves a backup is usable?
options: A recorded restore test that checks the data and measures time against the RTO
checks.explanation: Only a tested restore shows the data, keys, permissions and people all work.

modules.title: Cloud Logging, Monitoring and Detection
modules.purpose:
After the storage exposure, Kanem's head of risk asks whether security changes would be recorded and noticed in every cloud account. This module covers cloud audit logs, identity and sign-in events, central and protected log storage, managed threat detection and SIEM, and finding and closing monitoring gaps. You finish by assessing Kanem's logging coverage and writing its design.

**To complete this module:** finish all five lessons and pass the lab (80%), including the written design.
objectives: Identify management, data and identity events in each provider
Design central, protected log storage with appropriate retention
Use managed detection services and a SIEM to correlate and prioritise
Find and close monitoring gaps and keep detections working
assessmentCriteria: Assesses logging coverage correctly
Designs protected central logging with retention
Prioritises alerts defensibly
Writes a complete logging and monitoring design
modules.instructorNotes: Estimated time: 2.25 hours of lessons plus 1 hour of lab.

lessons.title: Cloud audit logs: management and data events
objectives: Distinguish management (control-plane) from data (data-plane) events
Identify where each provider records them and what is on by default
Define a logging baseline by data classification

checks.question: Which kind of event records someone reading an object in a storage bucket?
checks.explanation: Reading and writing data are data events, usually off by default.

checks.question: Which fields should a useful audit record provide? Select all that apply.
options: The identity that made the call
The source IP address and time
checks.explanation: Who, what, when, from where and whether it worked.

checks.question: Why use an organisation-wide trail or policy rather than configuring logging account by account?
options: It is required by every provider
New accounts are covered automatically and nobody can forget one
It is the only way to read logs
checks.explanation: Organisation-level configuration removes coverage gaps as the estate grows.

lessons.title: Identity and sign-in events
objectives: Find sign-in and identity-change events in each provider
Recognise identity signals that need review
Make identity logs meaningful through individual, clearly named identities

checks.question: Which identity events deserve review? Select all that apply.
options: Use of the root or Global Administrator account
A new access key created for an administrator
A change to a conditional-access policy
A user reading the staff handbook
checks.explanation: Top-level account use, new credentials and changes to protective policies are high-value signals.

checks.question: Why do shared accounts weaken sign-in logs?
options: The log cannot show which person acted
checks.explanation: Accountability needs one identity per person.

checks.question: What makes an unusual sign-in stand out?
options: A documented picture of what is normal for that identity
checks.explanation: Detections compare activity with an expected pattern.

lessons.title: Centralising and protecting logs
objectives: Design a central log archive outside workload accounts
Set retention with legal and compliance
Protect log integrity with immutability, validation and access control

checks.question: Why should logs be stored in a separate logging account?
options: Administrators of the workload accounts cannot alter or delete them
checks.explanation: Separation makes logs trustworthy evidence even if a workload account is compromised.

checks.question: Which measures protect log integrity? Select all that apply.
options: Giving all developers delete rights on the archive
Alerts on changes to logging configuration
checks.explanation: Integrity needs immutability, validation and tight control of the archive.

checks.question: Who should help decide log retention periods?
options: Legal and compliance, with the security team
checks.explanation: Retention must meet investigation, legal and regulatory needs.

lessons.title: Managed threat detection, SIEM and prioritisation
objectives: Explain the role of provider-managed detection services
Justify a SIEM for correlation across sources
Prioritise alerts with an explainable scheme
Use runbooks for consistent response

checks.question: What does a SIEM add beyond each provider's own detection service?
options: Correlation across cloud, identity, on-premises and endpoint sources, plus one alert queue and long-term search
checks.explanation: Correlation and a single queue are the main reasons for a SIEM.

checks.question: Which factors should raise an alert's priority? Select all that apply.
options: The identity involved is an administrator
The activity suggests impact, such as disabling logging
The alert arrived on a Tuesday
checks.explanation: Asset criticality, privilege, confidence, stage and exposure drive priority.

checks.question: What is the purpose of an alert runbook?
options: To make response consistent: what to check, who owns it, how to contain, when to escalate
checks.explanation: Runbooks give analysts a reliable first set of steps.

lessons.title: Monitoring gaps and detection engineering
objectives: Find gaps in sources, behaviours and past incidents
Treat detections as documented, versioned and tested code
Alert when logging itself breaks

checks.question: A new account was created last month and sends no logs. What kind of gap is this?
checks.explanation: Missing sources are the most basic gap, often caused by new accounts.

checks.question: Which practices belong to detection engineering? Select all that apply.
options: Documenting each detection's purpose and known benign cases
Testing detections against known-good and known-bad examples
Adding rules without ever reviewing them
checks.explanation: Detections are maintained like software.

checks.question: Why alert when a log source stops sending?
options: Silent logging failures create blind spots nobody notices
checks.explanation: Monitoring the monitoring prevents unnoticed gaps.

labs.title: Access review: least privilege for the invoice application
labs.summary: Review the invoice application's cloud permissions and usage evidence, find the escalation and evasion paths, write a least-privilege policy that passes 15 hidden access tests, and report the findings.

objectives: Identify excessive, escalation and defence-evasion permissions in a policy
Interpret access-activity evidence
Write a least-privilege policy that meets the application's needs exactly
Report an access-review finding to a security manager
content.scenario: Kanem Financial Services (fictional) has moved its **invoice application** to AWS. Before go-live, the security manager has asked you to review the permissions of its identity, `invoice-app-prod`. The application team says the policy was "copied from a tutorial to get it working". You have the policy, the application's documented needs and 90 days of access activity.
content.scope: Account 111122223333, region eu-west-1. All identifiers are synthetic. The policy simulator uses AWS-style identity-policy evaluation (explicit deny wins, otherwise an allow is needed); conditions are not evaluated.
content.instructions:
1. Read the three documents in the workspace.
2. Answer tasks 1–5.
3. In task 6, **edit the policy** so it grants exactly what the application needs. The grader runs 15 access requests you cannot see; all must be decided correctly.
4. In task 7, write the finding for the security manager. It is saved to your portfolio.

You need 80% to pass.

:::reveal Advanced challenge (optional)
Add an explicit Deny statement that protects invoices from deletion even if someone later attaches a broad policy to this identity. Does your policy still pass? Explain in your finding why an explicit deny is useful here, and what it cannot protect against (hint: other identities and bucket policies).
:::
content.simulationNotice: This is a simulation. All data is synthetic and generated by AMANIQ Academy for training. No real cloud accounts are used, nothing here costs money, and nothing you do leaves the platform.

documents.title: What the application needs (from the application team)
documents.body:
1. **Read** invoice PDFs: any object in the `kanem-invoices` bucket.
2. **Write** newly generated invoices, only under the `generated/` prefix of `kanem-invoices`.
3. **Decrypt** with the invoice KMS key `arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:111122223333:key/0000aaaa-11bb-22cc-33dd-444455556666`.
4. **Write logs** to the log group `/kanem/invoice-app` (create log streams and put log events).
5. Nothing else. Invoices must never be deleted by the application (7-year retention).

documents.title: Access activity for invoice-app-prod (last 90 days)
documents.body:
| Permission | Last used | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |

validator.debrief:
## Worked solution

**Excessive: S2, S4, S6, S7.** S2 (`s3:*` on `*`) lets the application read, change and delete every bucket, including payroll; S4 (`iam:PassRole` on `*`) and S6 (`ec2:*`) together are a privilege-escalation path; S7 lets anyone holding these credentials switch off or delete the audit trail. S1, S3 and S5 match needs 1, 4 and 3; need 2 (writing to `generated/`) was not granted at all, which is why the team added S2.

**Evidence:** on 28 February, from an address that is not Kanem's, the application identity launched an instance and passed it `kanem-admin`. The application never does this. Treat it as a probable credential compromise: escalate now, review CloudTrail around 02:41 UTC, find the instance and everything `kanem-admin` did, and deactivate the access key. (You will investigate this incident in module 9.)

### A policy that passes

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Sid": "ReadInvoices", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::kanem-invoices/*" },
    { "Sid": "WriteGenerated", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::kanem-invoices/generated/*" },
    { "Sid": "DecryptInvoices", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "kms:Decrypt", "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:111122223333:key/0000aaaa-11bb-22cc-33dd-444455556666" },
    { "Sid": "WriteLogs", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["logs:CreateLogStream", "logs:PutLogEvents"], "Resource": "arn:aws:logs:eu-west-1:111122223333:log-group:/kanem/invoice-app:*" },
    { "Sid": "NeverDeleteInvoices", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "s3:DeleteObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::kanem-invoices/*" }
  ]
}
```

The final Deny is optional (the advanced challenge). It protects against a broad policy being attached to this identity later, but not against other identities or the bucket policy: retention is better enforced with S3 Object Lock or a bucket policy as well.

### What a strong finding says

"The invoice application's identity can make itself an administrator (iam:PassRole on all roles plus full EC2), read and delete every S3 bucket, and turn off audit logging. Activity on 28 February shows this path being used from an external address (203.0.113.50) to obtain the kanem-admin role, which the application never does: this should be handled as a security incident today. Recommended: deactivate the access key; attach a role with the attached least-privilege policy; investigate CloudTrail for 28 February and all kanem-admin activity; add an organisation guardrail preventing CloudTrail from being stopped."

## What you have practised

This is a cloud access review: reading policy as the platform does, connecting permissions to attack paths (ATT&CK T1098, T1548.005), using evidence instead of opinion, and turning findings into actions a manager can approve. It maps to the Identity and Access Management domain of the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix and AWS IAM security best practices.

**Next:** module 3 applies the same thinking to cloud networks; module 9 picks up the 28 February activity as a full incident.

validator.debrief:
## Worked solution

| Responsibility | IaaS VM | PaaS DB | SaaS email | Serverless API |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Physical security | Provider | Provider | Provider | Provider |
| Hypervisor | Provider | Provider | Provider | Provider |
| Guest OS patching | **Customer** | Provider | Provider | Provider |
| Engine / runtime patching | **Customer** | Provider (shared: you plan major upgrades) | Provider | Provider (shared: you move off deprecated runtimes) |
| Application code | **Customer** | **Customer** (schema, queries, the apps using it) | Provider | **Customer** |
| Identities, access, MFA | **Customer** | **Customer** | **Customer** | **Customer** |
| Data | **Customer** | **Customer** | **Customer** | **Customer** |
| Network access rules | **Customer** | **Customer** | Shared (provider network; you set conditional access and sharing) | **Customer** / shared (API gateway authentication) |
| Backups and restore tests | **Customer** | Shared | Shared (retention; many organisations add third-party backup) | **Customer** / shared |
| Audit logging | Customer / shared | Customer / shared | Customer / shared | Customer / shared |

Both incidents were failures on the **customer** side: an unpatched guest OS in IaaS, and MFA available but not enabled in SaaS.

### A strong CFO briefing

"Moving to the cloud means the provider secures the buildings, hardware and platforms; Kanem still secures who can get in, what data we store and how every service is configured. For the reporting server we also keep patching its operating system; for the invoice database the provider patches the engine but we control access, backups and encryption keys; for email the provider runs the service but we must switch on MFA and manage sharing; for the loan API we own the code and its security settings. The providers' certificates prove their side is well run, not that ours is. We need named owners for MFA and access reviews, VM patching, backup and restore testing, and central logging before go-live."

## What you have practised

Deciding where responsibility sits is the first step of every cloud risk assessment, contract review and incident investigation. The same grid reappears in the capstone, when you design Kanem's full landing zone.

**Next:** module 2 tackles the responsibility at the top of every column: identity and access.

validator.debrief:
## Worked solution

**Classification:** rate sheets public; applications restricted; memos internal; exports confidential (restricted is also defensible, because they combine identity and financial data).

**Cause:** two settings together: the account-level public access block was switched off, and the bucket policy granted read access to everyone. Either control on its own would have prevented the exposure. Encryption did not help because the service decrypts for any request the policy authorises.

**Order of response:** block public access and remove the public statement first; preserve the access logs and the configuration history; scope exactly what was read anonymously (here, all 1,180 applications and both exports since 3 March); bring in the DPO and legal immediately, because data-protection law sets deadlines for notifying the regulator and affected people when an exposure is notifiable (the DPO decides; the NDPA 2023 includes a 72-hour regulator-notification duty for notifiable breaches); review how ticket WEB-1182 led to the change and what the deployer identity is allowed to do.

**Prevention:** enforce public access blocking with an organisation-level policy; publish rate sheets from the website or a separate public bucket; tag the bucket `data-classification = restricted`; consider a customer-managed key with decrypt limited to the loans application role; alert on any change to public access settings and on anonymous or unusual reads.

## What you have practised

This is a cloud data-exposure response: classify, find the cause, contain without destroying evidence, scope the impact, involve the right people early, and fix both the configuration and the process that produced it.

**Next:** module 5 builds the logging and detection that would have raised this on 3 March instead of a week later.

validator.debrief:
## Worked solution

**Coverage:** management events are present in three accounts but kept only 90 days in the same account; marketing-sandbox has nothing. Data access logging is needed in invoice-prod and loans-prod (confidential and restricted data), optional in invoice-dev (synthetic data). Threat detection is missing in loans-prod and marketing-sandbox.

**Design:** create a separate logging account with immutable storage, write-only access for sources and read access for security only; configure an organisation-wide trail and organisation policies so every new account is covered automatically and nobody can disable logging; keep audit records for at least 5 years, moving older logs to cheaper tiers; enable data-access logging for confidential and restricted stores; enable provider threat detection everywhere from a central security account.

**First alerts:** logging disabled anywhere; public access on confidential or restricted storage; privilege changes; top-level account use; and a log source going silent.

## What you have practised

Assessing logging coverage against data sensitivity and designing protected, central logging with retention and alerting: the foundation every investigation in module 9 depends on.

**Next:** module 6 secures the workloads themselves.

questions.prompt: Which question does authorisation answer?
questions.explanation: Authentication proves identity; authorisation evaluates policy for the requested action and resource.

options.text: Are you allowed to perform this action on this resource?
Which region is the request in?

questions.prompt: Which is a workload identity rather than a human identity?
questions.explanation: Managed identities, IAM roles used by services and Google service accounts are identities for workloads.

questions.prompt: No policy mentions s3:DeleteObject for a role. What happens when the role calls it?
questions.explanation: In AWS everything is denied unless a policy allows it.

questions.prompt: One policy allows s3:* on a bucket's objects and another denies s3:GetObject on the same objects. A GetObject request is:
questions.explanation: Explicit deny always wins in AWS policy evaluation.

options.text: Allowed, because allows are evaluated first
Denied, because an explicit deny overrides any allow
Allowed if both policies are in the same account

questions.prompt: An Allow statement has Resource "arn:aws:s3:::kanem-invoices/*". Which request does it NOT cover?
questions.explanation: The "/*" form matches objects in the bucket. Bucket-level actions use the bucket ARN without "/*".

options.text: None; it covers the whole bucket

questions.prompt: A user is granted the Google Cloud basic Editor role on a project. What is the main concern?
questions.explanation: Basic roles grant wide permissions and are inherited by resources in the project; predefined or custom roles are preferred.

options.text: Basic roles are very broad and apply to resources across the whole project
Editor only works in one region

questions.prompt: Which practices support least privilege? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Least privilege is built from documented needs, evidence of use and separation of environments.

options.text: Granting only the actions and resources a documented need requires
Removing permissions that usage data shows are never used
Granting Owner at subscription scope to speed up projects
Separating development and production into different accounts or subscriptions

questions.prompt: What distinguishes attribute-based access control (ABAC)?
questions.explanation: ABAC evaluates attributes of the principal, resource and request; RBAC grants permissions through roles.

options.text: Decisions use attributes such as tags, department or request context

questions.prompt: Why are temporary credentials preferred over long-lived access keys for workloads?
questions.explanation: Short-lived credentials from roles, managed identities or attached service accounts remove the stored secret.

options.text: They expire and rotate automatically, so a leaked copy has limited value and nothing is stored in code

questions.prompt: A valid access key is found in a public code repository. Which action comes first?
questions.explanation: Copies may already exist, so the key is disabled first; then investigate its use and replace it.

questions.prompt: A CI role trust policy accepts tokens from any repository on the CI platform. What is the risk?
questions.explanation: Federation must restrict the issuer, repository and branch that may assume the role.

options.text: Any repository owner on that platform could obtain the role's credentials

questions.prompt: An identity can call iam:PassRole on * and lambda:CreateFunction. How can it escalate?
questions.explanation: Passing any role to compute the identity controls lets it act with that role's permissions.

options.text: Create a function that runs with a highly privileged role and use it to act as that role

questions.prompt: Which Azure built-in roles can create role assignments by default?
questions.explanation: Contributor can manage resources but not grant access; Owner and User Access Administrator can write role assignments.

questions.prompt: Which controls reduce the risk of privileged cloud accounts? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Fewer standing privileges, guardrails above accounts and alerting on privilege changes are core controls. Shared accounts remove accountability.

options.text: Just-in-time activation of admin roles with a reason and time limit
Organisation-level guardrails that prevent disabling audit logging
Sharing one admin account so fewer accounts exist
Alerts on new role assignments, policy changes and break-glass sign-ins

questions.prompt: A managed relational database where the provider patches the engine is an example of:
questions.explanation: The provider runs the platform; the customer manages data, schema, access and configuration.

questions.prompt: In IaaS, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
questions.explanation: The customer manages everything from the guest OS upwards in IaaS.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of NIST's five essential characteristics of cloud computing?
questions.explanation: NIST lists on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

questions.prompt: Kanem keeps core banking on-premises and connects it to public-cloud workloads. Which deployment model is this?
questions.explanation: Hybrid combines deployment models connected so data and applications can move between them.

questions.prompt: What does spreading a workload across availability zones in one region protect against?
questions.explanation: Zones are isolated locations within a region; multi-region designs protect against regional outages.

options.text: The failure of a single data centre in the region

questions.prompt: What is the main security benefit of separate accounts, subscriptions or projects per environment?
questions.explanation: These containers are strong isolation boundaries with their own access and guardrails.

options.text: Isolation that limits what a compromise or mistake can reach

questions.prompt: Which responsibility is always the customer's, even in SaaS?
questions.explanation: Identities, data and the configuration you control are always the customer's.

questions.prompt: Which responsibilities are typically shared on a managed database service? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Shared tasks need both sides to do their part.

options.text: Backups: the provider takes them, the customer sets retention and tests restores
Engine updates: the provider applies them, the customer plans major upgrades
Encryption: the provider offers it, the customer controls key access

questions.prompt: What does a provider's SOC 2 report or ISO/IEC 27001 certificate tell a customer?
questions.explanation: Attestations are evidence about the provider, often with controls the customer must operate too.

options.text: That the customer's configuration is secure
That the provider's controls in scope were independently assessed

questions.prompt: A public storage bucket contains encrypted-at-rest files. Can anyone on the internet read them?
questions.explanation: Encryption at rest protects physical media; access control decides who gets decrypted data.

options.text: No, encryption at rest protects them
Yes, the service decrypts data for any request it authorises

questions.prompt: Which mechanism prevents any account in an AWS organisation from disabling CloudTrail?
questions.explanation: SCPs set maximum permissions for accounts in an organisation, including their administrators.

questions.prompt: Which NIST CSF 2.0 function was added to address organisational context, strategy, roles and policy?
questions.explanation: CSF 2.0 introduced Govern as a sixth function.

questions.prompt: Why is choosing a cloud region for customer personal data not just a technical decision?
questions.explanation: Legal and compliance input is needed; guardrails can then enforce the approved regions.

options.text: Data-protection law and regulators can restrict where data is stored and transferred

questions.prompt: Scanned national ID cards belong in which level of Kanem's scheme?
questions.explanation: Identity documents need the strongest controls.

questions.prompt: What is the right way to treat findings from a sensitive-data discovery tool?
questions.explanation: Discovery helps confirm classification and find surprises, but needs review.

options.text: As leads to review, since pattern matching has false positives and misses

questions.prompt: What does encryption at rest mainly protect against?
questions.explanation: Authorised API requests receive decrypted data.

options.text: Someone obtaining the physical or underlying storage media

questions.prompt: Why use a customer-managed key for restricted data?
questions.explanation: Reading needs both storage and key permissions.

options.text: It is required for all data
It adds an independent permission on key use and a detailed audit trail of decryption
It removes the need for access control

questions.prompt: In envelope encryption, what never leaves the key service?
questions.explanation: Data keys encrypt data; the master key protects the data keys inside the service.

questions.prompt: Which key-management practices reduce risk? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Key deletion makes data unrecoverable and must be tightly controlled.

options.text: Separate key administrators from key users
Log every use of restricted keys
Allow anyone to schedule key deletion

questions.prompt: Which is the safest place for a database password the application still needs?
questions.explanation: Secrets managers provide access control, logging and rotation.

options.text: In the repository with the code
In a plain environment variable in the deployment template
In a secrets manager, read at run time with the application's identity

questions.prompt: Which control overrides bucket policies that would grant public access?
questions.explanation: Public-access guardrails are designed to override permissive resource policies.

options.text: Account- or organisation-level public access prevention

questions.prompt: A file must be shared with one partner for 24 hours. What is the best option?
questions.explanation: Signed links are scoped to one object, expire and are logged.

options.text: A time-limited signed link to that object

questions.prompt: A restricted bucket is publicly readable. Which step comes first?
questions.explanation: Stop the exposure without destroying the evidence needed to scope it.

options.text: Block public access while preserving logs and configuration history
Rotate the encryption key and change nothing else

questions.prompt: Why should backups be immutable?
questions.explanation: Immutable storage protects backups even from administrators of the production account.

options.text: So that an attacker or mistake cannot delete or change them during the retention period

questions.prompt: What does an RTO of 4 hours mean?
questions.explanation: RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime; RPO is the acceptable data loss.

options.text: Four hours of data may be lost
The system must be restored within four hours

questions.prompt: What is the strongest evidence that backups will work in an emergency?
questions.explanation: Only a tested restore proves data, keys, permissions and procedures work together.

options.text: A recorded restore test in an isolated environment, timed against the RTO

questions.prompt: Which is a management (control-plane) event?
questions.explanation: Creating, changing and deleting resources and settings are management events.

options.text: Changing a storage bucket's access policy
Using a key to decrypt data

questions.prompt: Which kind of cloud logging is usually off by default and must be enabled for sensitive resources?
questions.explanation: Data events are high volume and usually need enabling per resource.

questions.prompt: Where are interactive and service-principal sign-ins recorded for Microsoft cloud services?
questions.explanation: Entra ID records sign-ins; the activity log records subscription operations.

questions.prompt: Which identity events are high-value signals? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Credential creation, privilege changes and top-level account use deserve review.

options.text: New credentials created for an identity
A user changing their profile photo
Use of the top-level administrator account

questions.prompt: What is the main reason for a separate log archive account?
questions.explanation: Separation preserves logs as trustworthy evidence.

options.text: Workload administrators, or an attacker controlling a workload account, cannot alter the logs

questions.prompt: Which feature proves CloudTrail log files have not been modified after delivery?
questions.explanation: Integrity validation detects modification or deletion of delivered log files.

questions.prompt: How should audit-log retention be decided?
questions.explanation: Retention must meet legal and investigative needs; tiers control cost.

options.text: With legal and compliance, based on investigation and regulatory needs

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a SIEM in a multi-cloud environment?
questions.explanation: Correlation across sources is the core value.

options.text: Correlating events from many sources in one place and one alert queue

questions.prompt: Which alert should normally be handled first?
questions.explanation: Weakened controls on restricted production data come first.

options.text: A failed sign-in to a development account
Audit logging disabled in a production account holding restricted data
A tag changed on a dev resource

questions.prompt: Which is a provider-managed threat detection service?
questions.explanation: GuardDuty, Defender for Cloud and Security Command Center provide managed findings.

questions.prompt: How do you make sure new accounts are logged from day one?
questions.explanation: Organisation-wide configuration removes manual steps.

options.text: Organisation-level trails and policies that apply to every account automatically

questions.prompt: What should happen before a new detection rule is deployed?
questions.explanation: Testing confirms it fires when it should and stays quiet when it should.

options.text: It is documented and tested against known-good and known-bad examples

questions.prompt: Why alert when a log source goes silent?
questions.explanation: Monitoring must detect its own failures.

options.text: A silent failure creates a blind spot nobody would otherwise notice
It is required by every provider
